Ageism is the word for prejudice, stereotyping, and discrimination directed at a person — or a group of people — solely because of their age.

Think of it like this: just as racism judges people unfairly based on their race, and sexism judges people unfairly based on their gender, ageism judges people unfairly based on how old they are. It is the assumption that a person's age tells you something meaningful about their worth, ability, intelligence, or value — and then treating them accordingly.

Most people, when they hear "ageism," picture the elderly. And yes, older people are the most common targets — they face assumptions that they are slow, out-of-touch, helpless, or a burden on society. But ageism can point in any direction.

Young people face it too. A 25-year-old professional might be dismissed in a meeting with the words, "You'll understand when you're older." A teenage girl's opinion might be waved away as immature before she even finishes her sentence. A young doctor might be doubted simply because they look young. This form — directed at younger people — is sometimes called adultism or youth discrimination, though it still sits comfortably under the umbrella of ageism.

So the key is this: ageism is not about which direction the bias flows. It is about the unfair act of using age as a measuring stick for a person's value or capability.

Ageism operates on three distinct but connected levels.

1. Stereotypes (What You Believe)
This is the foundation. A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified idea about a group of people. Ageist stereotypes include beliefs like: all old people are forgetful, rigid, and technologically helpless, or all young people are reckless, lazy, and inexperienced. These are broad, sweeping generalizations applied to an entire age group regardless of the reality of individual people.

2. Prejudice (How You Feel)
Prejudice is the emotional attitude that grows out of those stereotypes. It is the feeling of discomfort, pity, contempt, or dismissiveness that someone might feel toward a person simply because of their age — before even getting to know them. An employer who feels immediate doubt about hiring someone over 60 is experiencing an ageist prejudice, even if they never say it aloud.

3. Discrimination (What You Do)
This is where ageism moves from thought and feeling into action. Discrimination is the unfair treatment of a person based on their age. A company refusing to hire qualified people over 55, a doctor not explaining a medical condition fully to an elderly patient because they assume the patient "won't understand," or a bank refusing to issue a loan to a young adult without fair basis — all of these are acts of age-based discrimination.
Where Ageism Shows Up in Real Life

Ageism is not confined to one corner of life. It is woven into many different settings.

In the Workplace: This is one of the most documented arenas. Older workers may be passed over for promotions, forced into early retirement, or quietly pushed out and replaced with younger, cheaper employees. They might be seen as unable to learn new technology or adapt to change. On the flip side, a young employee's idea might be ignored in a meeting, or they might be given only trivial tasks because their colleagues assume they lack the experience to handle anything important.

In Healthcare: Older patients are sometimes undertreated because doctors assume that pain, depression, or cognitive decline is simply "a normal part of aging" rather than a real medical problem that deserves attention. Their complaints may be taken less seriously. Similarly, medical resources or experimental treatments are sometimes withheld from very old patients based purely on their age, with the assumption that their life is less worth saving or extending.

In Media and Culture: Think about how older people are portrayed on television, in advertisements, and in films. They are frequently shown as either comical and out-of-touch buffoons or as frail and dependent. Rarely are they depicted as complex, capable, vibrant individuals. Advertising overwhelmingly targets younger consumers and often makes aging itself seem like something shameful to be fought and hidden.

In Everyday Social Interactions: Ageism often lives in small, everyday moments. Talking extra slowly and loudly to an elderly person who has not indicated any hearing or cognitive difficulty. Finishing sentences for an older person without giving them the chance to speak. Saying to a young person, "You're too young to be stressed" or "That's an interesting opinion for someone your age." Using terms like "sweetie" or "dear" toward an elderly person in a way that infantilizes them. These moments may seem minor, but they accumulate and send a clear signal: your age makes you lesser.

In Laws and Institutions: Beyond individual behavior, ageism can be baked into the policies and systems of organizations, governments, and institutions. Mandatory retirement ages (when not justified by the genuine demands of a job), age caps in certain health insurance policies, or a legal system that historically dismissed the testimony of elderly witnesses — these are examples of systemic or institutional ageism.
Internalized Ageism: When You Believe It About Yourself

One of the most heartbreaking dimensions of ageism is internalized ageism — when a person absorbs and starts to believe the negative messages society sends about their own age group, and directs those beliefs at themselves.

An older person who says, "Oh, I'm too old to try that," about something they are physically and mentally perfectly capable of trying, may have internalized the cultural message that older people cannot learn or grow. A teenager who says, "Well, I'm just a kid, nobody will listen to me," has perhaps internalized the message that young voices don't matter. This is ageism doing its most insidious work — getting people to shrink themselves.

The damage caused by ageism is real and measurable, not merely a matter of hurt feelings.

For individuals, it can cause depression, loneliness, lower self-esteem, and even physical health decline. Research has found that older people who hold negative views about aging (often a product of internalizing ageist messages) tend to live shorter lives and recover more slowly from illness. Being excluded from the workforce strips older adults of financial security, purpose, and social connection. Young people who are constantly dismissed develop a sense of powerlessness.

For society as a whole, ageism is deeply wasteful. It squanders the wisdom, experience, and skills of older people by pushing them aside. It ignores the energy, fresh perspective, and potential of young people by not taking them seriously. A society that practices ageism is throwing away human potential at both ends of the age spectrum.

Unlike many other forms of bias, ageism has a few features that make it unusually slippery.

First, everyone ages. Ageism is the only form of discrimination where the discriminator will, if they live long enough, eventually become the target. Yet this rarely stops people from holding ageist views, partly because aging feels distant and abstract when you are young.

Second, ageism is often disguised as kindness. When someone takes an elderly person's grocery bag without asking, assumes they need help crossing the street, or makes decisions on their behalf without consulting them, it can look like care and concern. But it denies that person their autonomy and implicitly treats them as incapable — that is ageism, even when it is well-intentioned.

Third, ageist language is normalized. Phrases like "over the hill," "old fogey," "you're so mature for your age," or "OK Boomer" are so common that people rarely stop to question them. The casual nature of this language makes ageism easy to overlook as a serious issue.
The Simplest Way to Remember It

If you ever want to check whether something qualifies as ageism, ask yourself this one question:

"Would this thought, feeling, or action exist if the person were a different age?"

If the answer is no — if the only reason someone is being treated differently, judged, dismissed, or discriminated against is their age — then you are looking at ageism.

Ageism is the refusal to see a person as a full, complete human being — and instead, reducing them to a number.
